item.title: Internet Architecture Explained: One Story to Rule Them All
item.description:
A comprehensive guide to all high-frequency internet architecture concepts. At first glance, it seems overwhelming with concepts piled up, but at its core, it’s a continuous loop of fixing weaknesses and solving new problems.

1. Where It All Began: Monolithic Architecture

The story begins simply — you’ve just built a small website with very few users and minimal traffic. No need to overthink it. Keep it simple.

One server, running both the application and database, quickly set up with an open-source LNMP stack. You call it monolithic architecture.

1
2
3

┌─────────────────────┐
│     One Server       │
│  ┌───────────────┐  │
│  │  Application   │  │
│  ├───────────────┤  │
│  │    Database    │  │
│  └───────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────┘

Simple, straightforward, zero operational overhead — this is where all architectures begin.

2. Separating Application and Database

Business picks up, users increase, and the single server can’t keep up. Application and database constantly compete for CPU, memory, and IO, dragging each other down.

What to do? Add machines and split them up.

Separate application and database onto two servers: application server handles requests and business logic, database server stores data and performs IO operations. Each has its own responsibility, no interference, and availability improves.

3. High Concurrency Arrives: Clustering + Load Balancing

But the good times don’t last — user numbers explode again. A single application server can’t handle the load, and the database can’t withstand massive queries. The story reaches its climax — high concurrency arrives.

Even a maxed-out application server has limits. If it can handle 100 requests per second but 500 come in, what then?

500 ÷ 100 = 5, so you deploy five servers with identical code. You call it a cluster.

But there’s another problem: how to distribute traffic across each server? So you create a middle layer that evenly distributes requests to each application server. You call it load balancing.

Can’t handle the load? Add more machines → horizontal scaling. One goes down, traffic is automatically rerouted, others pick up the slack → high availability.

4. Database Becomes the New Bottleneck: Multi-Level Caching

The application handles the load, but a new problem emerges — massive requests penetrate through to the database, making it the new bottleneck.

You start researching how applications query databases:

  1. Application sends query request to database
  2. Database first checks the memory buffer for data
  3. Found → return directly; not found → go to disk, read it into memory buffer, then return to application

Key discovery: Reading from memory buffer is over 1000x faster than reading from disk.

Can we read everything from the memory buffer? No, it’s too small. What to do? Extract and expand the memory buffer! Put frequently accessed hot data there for quick queries without touching the database. You call it cache.

You design three levels of cache:

Level Description
Browser Cache Local to user, fastest
Application Server Local Cache In service instance memory, very fast
Distributed Cache (e.g., Redis) Centralized high-capacity memory, fast

User requests flow: Browser cache → Local cache → Distributed cache → Database.

The vast majority of requests are intercepted at the cache layer, never reaching the database. Query speed jumps from milliseconds to microseconds, and database pressure plummets. Even if the database goes down, the cache can hold for a while.

5. Read-Write Separation: Dividing Database Responsibilities

Caching solves hot reads, but write requests and non-hot reads still hit the database.

Databases have a characteristic: writes themselves aren’t slow, but multiple writes lock rows and tables, causing queues under high concurrency. Can we divide database responsibilities?

So you make the master database handle only writes and replica databases handle only reads, using data synchronization to keep master-replica consistency. You call it read-write separation.

In reality, internet systems are read-heavy, write-heavy. With one master and multiple replicas, read pressure is immediately distributed, and read-write blocking issues are completely resolved.

6. Massive Storage: Database Sharding

After running for years, data volume grows massive. Order tables, log tables become bloated — single database, single table can’t hold up. Database splitting becomes necessary.

Vertical Sharding: Split by business — user database, product database, order database, independent of each other.

Horizontal Sharding: Split one large table into multiple smaller tables, like hashing by UID to distribute pressure. With database middleware, it’s transparent to applications, no need to change lots of code.

7. CDN + Reverse Proxy: Fast and Secure

Your system users are nationwide. Some access it lightning-fast, others sluggish. Plus, application servers exposed directly on the public internet — too dangerous.

So you create two new tools:

CDN (Content Delivery Network): Deploy nodes across the country, pre-placing static resources at nodes closest to users, like a delivery station near your home. Users get the nearest node IP through domain resolution and fetch data — speed takes off.

Reverse Proxy: Placed between users and applications, public requests hit it first, then forward to internal application servers. Hides real servers, prevents attacks, handles traffic cleaning, permission verification — multi-purpose.

8. Complex Queries: Search Engines + NoSQL

Internet scenarios become increasingly complex. Traditional databases struggle with fuzzy queries, full-text search, and multi-dimensional statistics. Searching products with LIKE — painfully slow.

So you create two new tools:

Search Engine (e.g., Elasticsearch): Uses inverted indices for instant search responses.

NoSQL Database (e.g., MongoDB, HBase): Stores unstructured and semi-structured data, high concurrency, easy to scale.

The system evolves from simple CRUD to supporting complex retrieval and analysis.

9. Distributed Architecture: Split It Up!

Business grows, your website evolves from a small e-commerce site into a massive platform combining users, products, and orders.

All functionality crammed into one application becomes what’s known as a monolithic application. Problems follow:

  • Changing one line of user code requires full deployment
  • Multiple developers modifying code daily, constant conflicts
  • Want to scale orders? Must scale the entire application — resources wasted

What to do? Split it!

Along business boundaries, cut this big application piece by piece: users, products, orders become independent small systems. Each system deploys, releases, and scales independently, no interference. You call it distributed architecture.

But new problems emerge after splitting — systems are separated, how to call each other? So you create RPC (Remote Procedure Call), making cross-machine service calls as simple as calling local code.

Services multiply, call chains grow complex, quick target finding becomes a challenge. So you create a manager — Service Registry and Discovery Center: new services register, anyone needing to call finds them here.

10. Message Queues: Decoupling and Peak Shaving

Services call each other, wait for each other — one service gets stuck, the entire chain blocks. Traffic spikes, avalanche occurs.

What to do? Can we stop services from waiting on each other?

So you create a super-capacity smart mailbox: services don’t need to wait for immediate replies, just throw messages in and continue their work. Anyone needing it fetches it themselves. You call it message queue (MQ).

Now services are completely decoupled, no dragging each other down. A service temporarily goes down, messages aren’t lost — process them gradually after recovery. Traffic surges, store requests first and digest at system capacity — peak shaving.

11. Microservices Architecture: Splitting Even Finer

After using distributed architecture for years, you discover new problems — split, yes, but not fine enough.

Take the user system: it still contains login, profile, membership, address… a big blob. Different teams want different tech stacks — some Java, some Go — mixing in one system doesn’t work. Membership module needs scaling for promotions, must scale the entire user system, money and resources wasted.

What to do? Keep splitting!

Following the principle of one service does one thing, split smaller and finer:

  • Login becomes a standalone service
  • Membership becomes a standalone service
  • Payment becomes a standalone service
  • …

Each small service develops, releases, and scales independently, using whatever tech stack you want. You call this more extreme architecture microservices architecture.

When promotions hit, the hottest services like orders and payments get ten times the machines, other quiet services untouched — zero resource waste. A service bug affects only that small feature, never drags down the entire site. Dozens of teams, each managing their own service, no interference — development efficiency soars.

Of course, with benefits come challenges — call relationships like spider webs, add distributed tracing to pinpoint slow services instantly; fear of cascading failures, add rate limiting, circuit breaking, degradation for automatic protection; too many services to manage, implement service governance: unified monitoring, logging, permissions all organized clearly.

12. Containerization: Package Once, Run Anywhere

Microservices are truly useful, but operations engineers cry.

Services split finer and finer, from a few applications to hundreds of microservices. Each service online needs environment setup, dependency installation, parameter tuning — slightest difference causes “works on my machine, not on server” mystic bugs. Before promotions, emergency scaling of hundreds of machines, setting up environments one by one can’t keep up; after promotions, scaling down requires cleaning one by one — efficiency ridiculously low.

What to do?

Can we package the service and its required runtime environment together into a sealed box that runs directly on any server?

So you create a new tool — no more environment setup. Package each microservice’s code, dependencies, configuration, and environment into an image — package once, run anywhere, completely solving the century-old problem of environment inconsistency. You call it Docker container.

13. Container Orchestration: Kubernetes the Manager

But problems persist — hundreds or thousands of containers, who manages them?

So you bring in an all-powerful manager. It arranges container resources, schedules container placement, auto-scales. You call it Kubernetes (K8s):

  • Traffic spikes → auto-add containers
  • Traffic drops → auto-remove containers
  • Container crashes → auto-restart
  • You don’t need to manage any of it

14. Cloud Native: The New Era of Architecture

Still not done — even with K8s, you still buy servers and maintain data centers. Preparing heaps of machines for promotions that sit idle daily — too wasteful.

So you move your system to a cloud platform.

The cloud platform is like an infinite resource pool — CPU, memory, bandwidth, apply anytime, use anytime, release when done, pay as you go. Underlying infrastructure is completely transparent; you only focus on business.

Your architecture enters a new era — you call it cloud native.

15. Story Summary: Architecture Evolution Panorama

From a small server to elastic, automated, highly available, infinitely scalable modern architecture — no matter how business grows or traffic explodes, it stands firm.

Stage Problem Solved Core Solution
Monolithic Building from scratch One server does everything
App/DB Separation Resource contention Split into two, each with its own role
Cluster + Load Balancing High concurrency Multiple servers + traffic distribution
Multi-Level Caching Query performance, DB pressure Browser → Local → Distributed cache
Read-Write Separation DB read/write blocking Master writes, replicas read
Database Sharding Massive storage Vertical sharding + horizontal sharding
CDN + Reverse Proxy Access speed, security Nearby access + hide real servers
Search + NoSQL Complex queries Inverted indices + unstructured storage
Distributed Architecture Business bloat, code maintenance Split by business, RPC communication
Message Queues Service coupling, traffic impact Async decoupling + peak shaving
Microservices Team collaboration, extreme elasticity One service does one thing
Containerization (Docker) Environment inconsistency Package once, run anywhere
Container Orchestration (K8s) Operations cost Auto-scheduling + elastic scaling
Cloud Native Resource utilization Pay as you go, transparent infrastructure

Three Core Architect Mindsets

Finally, three takeaways. Understand them, and you can design good architectures.

One: There’s no best architecture, only the architecture that best fits the business.

Startups shouldn’t jump straight to microservices. Monolith is fine — business drives architecture, not the other way around.

Two: The essence of architecture evolution: trade space for time, trade complexity for performance.

Adding machines, components, layers — all to handle bigger traffic, higher concurrency.

Three: Always center on five goals: high performance, high availability, scalability, extensibility, and security.

These five goals are the North Star for all architecture decisions.

From a small server to cloud-native architecture handling tens of millions of concurrent requests, every step is traceable, every step solves real problems. This is internet architecture.
